title: Should You Use Lifting Straps? When They Help Your Pulls and When to Skip Them
description: Trials show straps add reps and preserve grip on heavy pulls for women and men alike — without boosting muscle recruitment. When straps earn their place, when to skip them, and the honest answer on grip.

bestFor: Women who lift and watch their grip give out before their back or hamstrings on heavy pulls — and want the trial evidence on what straps actually add (and don't), the honest answer on whether straps weaken grip, and a clear protocol for when to strap, when to skip, and how to train grip alongside them.
body:
On heavy rows, RDLs, and deadlifts, there's a moment every lifter knows: the target muscle still has reps left, but your fingers are opening like a claw machine. Straps promise to remove that ceiling — and the debate around them copies the belt debate exactly, with gatekeeping in both directions. One camp says straps are cheating that will leave your grip weak forever. The other straps every pull from warm-ups to wrist curls.

The research is surprisingly clear about what straps do and don't do, and it supports a narrower use than either camp advertises. This article covers what straps actually change on heavy pulls, what the trials found (including one in women specifically), the honest answer to "won't straps weaken my grip?", and where they fit in a training week.

## What Straps Actually Do

Lifting straps are fabric loops that attach your wrists to the bar, converting your grip from an open pinch into a closed hook. Mechanically, they remove the grip — forearm strength and finger friction — as the limiting link in a pull, so the target muscle (lats, traps, hamstrings, glutes) becomes the thing that ends the set.

That's a real and useful change, because grip strength doesn't scale with goal-muscle strength. As your pulls get heavier, your back and hips can outpace your forearms, and without straps, grip turns into a hidden governor: sets end early, velocity drops, and the muscle you're training gets less work than the loading says it should.

## What the Research Shows

The best evidence is recent, and one trial is specific to this site's audience. A 2023 study in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research had ten experienced women perform three sets of as many repetitions as possible at 80 percent of their deadlift max, with and without straps. With straps, the women completed significantly more total repetitions, lost significantly less grip strength across the sets, and showed no negative change in barbell velocity. The conclusion was straightforward: straps let women do more pulling work with grip fatigue substantially reduced.

A 2021 trial in Physiology & Behavior (in men, at 80 percent of max for four-by-four deadlifts) found the same pattern plus useful extras: straps preserved grip strength between sets and sped up grip recovery, improved perceived grip security and power, and lowered perceived exertion — but with one important nuance. When the lifters loaded the bar to their *with-straps* max, bar velocity actually dropped below the unstrapped condition. Straps let you do more work at your real strength level; they don't make you stronger, and loading as if they did just makes every rep slower.

What straps don't do matters as much. A 2026 exploratory review in the International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance found no consistent evidence that straps increase muscle recruitment or improve performance in pulling and back exercises generally — and noted that claims about straps' long-term training effects, in either direction, are hypotheses rather than findings. The review's core distinction is worth memorizing: straps ergogenically extend hard set work; they are not a growth technology.

## When Straps Help

The evidence supports straps in a narrow band of situations:

- **When grip fails before the target muscle.** Heavy RDLs, barbell rows, shrugs, and top-set deadlifts — whichever [bar and stance you pull](/blog/trap-bar-vs-conventional-vs-sumo-deadlift) — where your hands open before your back is done. This is the textbook case, and the trials above are its proof.
- **High-rep pulling work.** Grip fatigue accumulates faster than muscle fatigue at higher reps; the women's trial showed exactly this at sets to failure.
- **Late in a session**, when grip is pre-fatigued and you still have meaningful pulling work left.
- **Occasional heavy attempts** where you want the target system, not your fingers, to be the limiter.

## When to Skip Them

Skip straps in equally specific situations:

- **When grip is the training goal.** Deadlift grip strength, farmer carries, holds, and thick-bar work exist to train the grip — strapping them defeats the purpose. If your grip is the reason your deadlift stalls, the fix is a [grip program](/blog/grip-strength-training-women-who-lift), not softer fabric.
- **Warm-ups and moderate loads.** Strapping sets that your grip handles comfortably trains nothing and helps nothing.
- **Any pull where the grip challenge is the point** — and for most general-strength lifters, that includes at least some heavy deadlift work every training cycle, left unstrapped on purpose.
- **Competition pulls.** Straps are banned in powerlifting deadlifts; if you compete, some training must happen exactly as you'll compete.

## Won't Straps Weaken My Grip?

This is the fear that keeps people white-knuckling rows, and the honest answer has two parts. First: there is no good evidence that using straps on heavy pulls reduces grip strength — the women's trial directly measured grip across sets and found straps *preserved* it, and the review found no chronic-effect evidence in either direction. The "straps rot your grip" claim is gym folklore, not data.

Second, and more useful: grip strength responds to direct training, so you don't have to choose between big pulls and a strong grip. Dedicated grip work — holds, carries, and targeted forearm training — a couple of times per week more than covers the stimulus your strapped pulls didn't provide (and hand care counts too: [torn calluses](/blog/lifting-weights-with-torn-callus) undermine grip all on their own). Straps aren't an alternative to grip training; they're what lets both exist without competing for the same sets.

One caution belongs here: straps change which muscle limits the set, and they don't fix anything that isn't grip — a back that hurts on pulls needs the [pain-guided modification path](/blog/lower-back-pain-deadlift-modifications), not better fabric.

## How to Use Them Well

Loop the strap around your wrist, wrap the free end around the bar *toward your body* (against the direction the bar rolls out of your fingers), and pull the wrap snug — a loose strap is a slipping strap. Use them on working sets only, starting with the heaviest one or two, exactly the same way the [belt article](/blog/should-women-use-a-lifting-belt) suggests introducing a belt. And if grip is chronically your limiter on pulls, add direct grip work to your program rather than simply strapping everything forever — the goal is a grip that limits you rarely, not straps that hide it always.

## What to Do Next

- **Grip fails before your back or hamstrings on heavy pulls:** use straps on your heaviest sets and add two direct-grip sessions per week.
- **Grip keeps up comfortably:** skip them — you're getting free grip training every pull.
- **Training for powerlifting:** strap your accessory pulls, keep competition-style deadlifts unstrapped.
- **Unsure where your grip actually stands:** test it — one heavy unstrapped set tells you more than any article, including this one.

## The Bottom Line

Straps are an extension of hard set work, not a shortcut around it. The trials show they add repetitions, preserve grip, and lower effort perception on heavy pulls — for women and men alike — without harming velocity or, per the best available review, without any evidence they boost muscle recruitment or long-term gains. Use them when grip is the limiter and the target muscle isn't, train your grip on its own schedule, and the strap debate dissolves into what it always was: a tool question with a per-session answer.
